perforated appendix with a 51×31×26 mm collection and surrounding fat stranding
bulky multi-station mediastinal lymphadenopathy contiguous with soft tissue thickening enveloping the right lower and middle lobe bronchi
4-hour history of acute right lower-quadrant abdominal pain
perforated appendix with a 51×31×26 mm collection and surrounding fat stranding
bulky multi-station mediastinal lymphadenopathy contiguous with soft tissue thickening enveloping the right lower and middle lobe bronchi

concepts.why: The patient presented with acute right lower-quadrant abdominal pain and was found to have a perforated appendix with surrounding fat stranding on CT scan.
The patient has a history of prostate cancer in remission and was found to have innumerable hepatic nodules and bulky multi-station mediastinal lymphadenopathy on CT scan.
The patient presented with fever, tachycardia, and pulmonary consolidation on CT scan.
The patient was found to have a thickened, woody sigmoid colon and innumerable hepatic nodules on CT scan, suggesting possible colorectal cancer with metastasis.

rationales.F05: Prostate cancer in remission increases the likelihood of metastatic prostate cancer.
rationales.F10: Perforated appendix is a strong indicator of appendicitis.
rationales.F11: Innumerable hepatic nodules suggest metastatic disease, which could be related to prostate cancer or colorectal cancer.
rationales.F12: Bulky multi-station mediastinal lymphadenopathy is highly suggestive of metastatic cancer, which could be related to prostate cancer or other primary cancers.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient presented with acute right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, peritonism, and a perforated appendix with surrounding fat stranding, which are strong evidence for appendicitis. While metastatic prostate cancer is also a possible diagnosis given the patient's history and the presence of innumerable hepatic nodules and bulky lymphadenopathy, the immediate cause of the patient's acute presentation and death was the perforated appendix.
